newsitem.title: FRANCE: Seguin says France needs growth, no inflation risk.
newsitem.headline: Seguin says France needs growth, no inflation risk.

text.p: French parliament speaker Philippe Seguin, seen as a Gaullist rival to Prime Minister Alain Juppe, called on Friday for a monetary stimulus and more realistic exchange rates to promote faster economic growth.

Criticising the orthodox monetary policies of the Bank of France and the German Bundesbank, Seguin said European financial authorities continued to act as if inflation, not unemployment, were the main enemy.

"Governments want lower interest rates to fight unemployment more effectively. But the radical cut that is necessary is refused in the name of fighting inflation," Seguin told a Gaullist RPR party seminar in Troyes, southeast of Paris.
"The problem is that unemployment is a reality, while the risk of inflation is no longer current in our country."

"It is urgent to ensure that the march towards a single European currency is not incompatible with growth...The aim is to ensure vigorous growth through reasonable monetary stimulation, and to return to realistic exchange rates both within Europe and towards the rest of the world," he said.

A former opponent of the Maastricht treaty on European Union reluctantly reconciled to the single currency, Seguin appeared to be a voice in the wilderness, since President Jacques Chirac stressed last week he would stick to austere economic policies meant to cut public deficits and peg the franc to the mark.
By coincidence, Socialist opposition parliamentary floor leader Laurent Fabius issued a similar call for a change of economic policy in an article in the daily Le Monde on Friday.

After a "frank discussion" with Germany, France should "put in place a more flexible monetary policy, a more dynamic economic policy...in place of a government strategy aimed against inflation which no longer exists", Fabius said.
